item.title: Agent Guardrails Belong in Config, and Config Needs Tests
item.author: Mike Dabydeen
item.content:encoded:
When an AI agent can run shell commands in your pipeline, its permissions are infrastructure. They should be declared where reviewers look, versioned with the agent, and tested on every change. Docker Agent gets the first two right. The third is up to you, and when I wrote the tests, one widely used permission pattern failed in a way worth knowing about.Docker Agent is Docker's open-source runtime for teams of agents. A team is a config file: models, agents, which agents each one may delegate to, which tools each may use, and the policy around all of it. You run it with docker agent run crew.yaml.My test project, release-gate-crew, is a release gate for container services. A lead agent delegates to a container auditor and a pipeline auditor, then hands their findings to a scribe that writes a PASS/BLOCK report. The sample service under review is deliberately bad: an unpinned base image, a secret in , a privileged container with the Docker socket mounted, and a workflow that checks out untrusted code with write permissions.Every control sits in the same file as the agents:agents: container_auditor: model: worker instruction_file: prompts/container_auditor.md toolsets: - type: filesystem allow_list: ["./target"] # read scope - type: shell
runtime: safety: restricted # unattended: deny anything not allowed
permissions: allow: ["read_file", "shell:cmd=grep -n *"] deny: ["shell:cmd=*curl*", "shell:cmd=*&&*", "shell:cmd=*;*", "shell:cmd=*|*"]
budget: max_cost: 0.50 # one pot shared by every agent max_time: 10m A file hides and key files from every agent. The same team also exists as , because Docker Agent reads HCL too, and platform teams that live in Terraform may prefer it.Testing guardrails without a modelGuardrails are deterministic, so they should be testable without paying for tokens or tolerating model variance. I wrote a scripted, OpenAI-compatible stub model in Go and pointed every agent at it through a config flavor. The stub plays a fixed sequence per agent. It delegates, reads files, and then deliberately tries things the config should refuse.A Go integration test drives the real binary against both config files and checks nine written requirements. The runtime's own responses:excluded by .agentsignorePipeline auditor reads a file outside outside the allowed directories (./target)Scribe writes denied by restricted safety mode, no promptgrep -n FROM target/Dockerfile && curl --versiondenied by permissions configurationAll of that held, for YAML and HCL alike.The pattern that didn't holdPermission rules are globs matched against the whole command string, and matches spaces. So consider the prefix style common in examples:permissions: allow: ["shell:cmd=grep -n *"] deny: ["shell:cmd=curl *"] The command grep -n FROM target/Dockerfile && curl --version begins with , so the allow rule matches. It does not begin with , so the deny rule misses. Deny is evaluated first, finds nothing, then allow approves. In my test, curl ran and printed its version banner. The safety mode did not stop it, because an explicit allow outranks the mode.Docker's documentation says permissions are client-side and not a security boundary, and it recommends sandbox mode for isolation. I agree with that framing. The risk is practical: prefix rules look precise, and they are what most people will copy.Four changes close the gap:Deny shell operators: , , , backticks and .Match denied binaries anywhere: , not .Allow one narrow command per agent that needs a shell.Use , which runs the team in a Docker Sandboxes VM, for anything you don't fully trust.My suite keeps a test that reproduces the bypass. If a future release starts parsing compound commands, that test will fail and tell me to revisit the advice.The filesystem toolset is unrestricted by default. Set on every one.A config pulled from a registry can declare runtime.safety: autonomous. Your own flag or user settings take precedence only if you set them.Sub-agents receive only the task text the lead writes, inside a block. Good isolation, but the lead must pass along everything a specialist needs.The project moves quickly: 17 releases in September 2026. Pin the version in CI and disable telemetry there with .What the stub can't tell youNone of this measures review quality. A scripted stub proves the harness, not the judgement. The repository includes three cases for that: block the flawed sample, refuse to reveal the secret, and refuse to claim an edit. They need real model keys and a container runtime, and I haven't run them yet.That split is the main lesson I'd take to any agent platform. Test the guardrails deterministically on every push. Evaluate the model's judgement separately, with repeated runs, before you trust a gate decision.

item.title: Using Cypress Cloud CLI and Test Replay for AI-Assisted CI Debugging
item.author: Raju Dandigam
item.content:encoded:
A checkout test fails in CI with this message:expected '[data-cy="cart-total"]' to have text '$45.00' The screenshot shows . An AI assistant can invent several plausible explanations: the discount request failed, React rendered stale state, the selector found the wrong cart, or the assertion ran early.Plausible is not the same as supported.The quality of AI-assisted debugging depends less on how confidently the assistant explains the screenshot and more on whether it can inspect the evidence that produced it.Recorded CI and live local debugging are different surfacesCypress now exposes two useful but distinct agent workflows: A live, local open-mode Cypress session; Run and verify a change during development Completed Cloud runs and Test Replay data; Reconstruct an existing CI failureI have written separately about giving an agent access to a live Cypress session. This workflow starts at the opposite end: the failure already happened, perhaps only in CI, and the recorded attempt is the evidence.The Cypress Cloud CLI returns JSON for runs, specs, tests, commands, network requests, and console events. The local Test Replay viewer is available through in CLI version or newer.Start with a deliberately small evidence packetThe current documentation requires Node.js or newer and recommends using the latest CLI. Install it, record the resolved version, and pin that exact version in repeatable CI automation after validation:npm install --global @cypress/cloud@latest cy-cloud version cy-cloud status For a failed run, the shortest useful path is:cy-cloud run list \ --projectId <projectId> \ --branch main \ --status failed \ --limit 1
cy-cloud test list \ --projectId <projectId> \ --runNumber <runNumber> \ --status failed
cy-cloud replay timeline \ --testId <testId> \ --commands \ --aroundFailure 5 \ --network \ --logs That packet answers four questions:Which commands immediately preceded it?Which XHR or fetch activity overlapped the failure?Did the application log a related error?Do not begin by dumping an entire organization's run history into an agent. Scope the query to one project, run, test, attempt, and timeline window.Suppose the test failed on attempt one and passed on attempt two. A screenshot from the failed attempt tells us the symptom. Comparing the attempts can expose the first causal difference.cy-cloud replay timeline \ --testId <testId> \ --attempt 1 \ --commands --network --logs \ > attempt-1.json
cy-cloud replay timeline \ --testId <testId> \ --attempt 2 \ --commands --network --logs \ > attempt-2.json Imagine the relevant entries reduce to:, response at 1,240 ms; , response at 310 ms 820 ms; 760 ms; none; noneThe evidence does not yet prove whether the product or test is wrong, but it eliminates several guesses. The assertion can run before the successful response. The next review question is whether the UI should block until the response arrives, or whether the test failed to wait for an application event that defines completion.The timeline gives structure. The local replay viewer lets you inspect the recorded DOM and styles around one command:cy-cloud replay view open --testId <testId>
cy-cloud replay view move \ --testId <testId> \ --attempt 1 \ --pin '<commandId>|before'
cy-cloud replay view inspect \ --testId <testId> \ --selector '[data-cy="cart-total"]'
cy-cloud replay view move \ --testId <testId> \ --attempt 1 \ --pin '<commandId>|after' This is more diagnostic than asking an agent to infer causality from the final screenshot. It can see whether an earlier command changed an attribute, collapsed a container, or left the DOM stale. requires a Chromium-family browser and Cloud CLI or newer. Because Cloud CLI is Beta, scripts should pin a compatible version and treat output schemas as versioned dependencies.Give the agent a diagnostic contractAn unrestricted prompt such as “fix this test” encourages the assistant to optimize for a green run. It may add a hard wait, broaden a selector, remove an assertion, or mask a product regression.A better task is bounded:Analyze attempt-1.json and attempt-2.json for test <testId>.
1. Identify the first material difference before the failed assertion. 2. Cite the relevant command, network, or console event IDs. 3. Classify the likely cause as product, test synchronization, test data, environment, or unknown. 4. Propose the smallest code change, but do not edit files. 5. Do not add fixed waits or weaken the business assertion. 6. List the local verification commands and one negative control. The request separates observation, diagnosis, proposal, and execution. A human can reject the classification before any code changes.Credential locality is not the whole security modelCloud CLI access follows the organizations, teams, projects, and roles available to the authenticated Cypress Cloud user. OAuth is recommended locally; a personal access token can be supplied through in CI. Stored credentials are owner-readable on the local machine.Those are useful controls, but they do not mean every AI environment is automatically safe. If an agent can read arbitrary environment variables, home-directory files, or shell output, it may reach more than intended.Use the ordinary least-privilege questions:Which Cypress Cloud user or service identity is authenticating?Which projects can it read?Can the agent execute arbitrary shell commands?Where are downloaded replay data and screenshots cached?Can captured network bodies contain secrets or personal data?When are local artifacts deleted?Cypress supports masking and redaction for Test Replay network data; configure those boundaries before making replay evidence broadly available.Verification remains a separate stepAfter reviewing a proposed fix, run the affected spec locally. A useful sequence is:reproduce with the same fixture or a sanitized equivalent;apply the smallest reviewed change;run the original failure case;run a negative control that should still fail;inspect the behavior, not just the exit code;push only after the evidence agrees.The negative control matters. If changing the selector makes the test pass even when the discount is not applied, the “fix” destroyed the test.Remove runner drift with a pinned containerBefore blaming the test or product, rerun the candidate change in the same declared Node and browser environment. An official or image can make that boundary repeatable, but only when you pin a full version tag or digest:export CYPRESS_IMAGE='cypress/browsers@sha256:<approved-digest>' docker compose run --rm \ -e CYPRESS_SPEC='cypress/e2e/checkout.cy.ts' \ cypress The Compose service should run the same repository revision and application fixture used in the investigation. Record docker image inspect "$CYPRESS_IMAGE", , , and the selected browser with the evidence packet. A green result in a different image is not a reproduction; it is a new experiment.What this workflow does not proveRecorded Test Replay evidence describes one captured run. It does not prove that a failure is statistically representative or that the proposed patch is correct. A passing retry can differ because of data, timing, infrastructure, or an actual product race.Cloud CLI is also not an autonomous remediation system. It is a read-oriented evidence interface. Code changes, approval, and verification remain responsibilities of your development workflow.Ask AI to explain bounded evidence before asking it to change code.That turns the assistant from a confident guesser into a supervised participant in a debugging process whose claims can be reviewed

item.title: Agent Security & Identity (Part 2): Who Are You, Who's Your Agent, And What Should They Be Allowed?
item.author: Alejandro Saucedo
item.content:encoded:
This is a 2-part series on agent identity and security: who the user is, who the agent is, and what each of them should be allowed to reach. Part 2 runs the design end to end on a cluster, with two users, two agents, a tool, a model and a third-party service.In Part 1, I designed how agent identity can work on a platform where agent-delegation is enabled, and how we decide (+ enforce) what they and their users are allowed to reach. In this second and final part I deploy that design on a cluster and check whether it actually holds up.In this Part 2 blog post, I go through a hands-on use-case with 2 users of the same agent platform at the same company: Alice is in the group and Bob is in the group. Throughout this I will show the good, the bad and the ugly of agentic identity and security, especially when dealing with autonomous agents, and with users delegating permissions to an agent.The walkthrough answers 4 questions:Does an agent requesting a tool for a user in the wrong group actually get refused?When an agent calls its own tool and model, how do we authorize (+ verify) the hops?What happens to an autonomous agent that has no user behind it at all?When Alice asks for a 3rd party service (i.e. github) via an agent, does the request go out as Alice?Most of what I learnt came from the requests that got denied (+ from the complexities and lessons learned), so you'll see plenty of those below.Everything below runs on a local KIND cluster against the public Agentic Identity Broker release, pinned at . On a local cluster GitHub is a mock, so the consent screen gets completed automatically instead of in a browser, but every identity and access-control decision you'll see is real.Here's a quick refresher of what we covered in Part 1 before we run it.I started with the challenges we all phase when agents have to access 3rd party services on behalf of a user. Here I showed how just giving an API token falls short, as you can't tell which user an action was for, it has more access than any single user needs, and you can't revoke it for just one user.Fixing that needed a component that holds each user's own third-party credential, obtained with their consent. The Agentic Identity Broker does exactly that, so I adopted it instead of writing my own.Then I separated the 2 identities that every protected call carries. The is the human the work is being done for, and the is the agent doing the work. This is how the system enforces resource access on the actor and use the subject for what the user personally delegated, which keeps permissions correct when agents call other agents.Finally I made 6 architecture decisions, and 3 of them matter most for what follows:One gateway on every hop, plus a NetworkPolicy so nothing can go around itChecks in the agent runtime, a sidecar per workload, a service meshHow authorization is modelledOne explicit for who may enter an agent, with the agent's own dependencies derived from its spec, all evaluated by KAOS's own Open Policy Agent decision pointA policy language as the authoring surface, or the broker answering the decisionKAOS owns the integration; the broker and the identity provider run as their own releasesThe platform installing and lifecycle-managing its own brokerThat third row is why this walkthrough has both a broker and Keycloak in it. The broker holds the delegated third-party credentials and performs the exchange, and the gateway attaches the returned credential to the outbound request. Keycloak proves who the human is, carries the group membership the rules match on, and registers each agent as its own client so the broker can tell which agent is asking.Now let's build the cluster and see it work.The is the set of components that establish identity and decide the rules. Apart from the gateway, none of them carry your agents' actual traffic; they answer the 3 questions from part 1 about it. Here they are on one map. The greyed pieces belong to section 5 and can be ignored for now.There are quite a few components in this overview, so let's walk through them:: This is the single gateway every request passes through, including agent-to-tool, agent-to-model and agent-to-agent calls, which is what makes it a mesh.: Authenticates users, proves who they are and which groups they belong to; supports OIDC compatible services so we use Keycloak here.: Gives each agent their identity through secure credentials; the default uses k8s Service Accounts, but also supports OIDC compatible services; we also configure Keycloak in this example.: This is the authorization (authz) service that KAOS uses to allow/deny requests based on the "user" calling the "agent" accessing the "resource".Agent Impersonation Service: Lets an agent act on an outside service (like GitHub) as the user by exchanging third-party tokens (github/slack/etc) through a consent mechanism. The concrete tool I use is the Agent Identity Broker (AIB), and it gets its own section, section 5.: This component synchronises auth & identity bidirectionaly; it registers the KAOS resources on upstream auth services, and injects identities and secrets across KAOS resources.Before I show how this all fits together with an example, let's configure the kubernetes cluster with this setup.1.1 Install it in one commandI use the KAOS CLI to install the Gateway Mesh, User Auth, Agent Auth, the KAOS Authz Service, the KAOS Operator, and the Agent Identity Broker (AIB).This command wires everything together in a new cluster:kaos system install \ --gateway-strict \ # Traffic can only go through gateway --authz-enabled \ # KAOS Authorization service enabled --user-auth keycloak \ # Use Keycloak for User auth (alt: OIDC) --agent-auth keycloak \ # Use Keycloak for Agent Auth (alt: Service Accts. or OIDC) --token-exchange-enabled \ # Use AIB for token exchange
# Other flags --wait \ # Block until everything is ready --create-cli-config # In-folder config file for cli kaos system install --help lists everything else (image tags, resource limits, replica counts, realm names, observability backends); the Helm values behind each flag are shown per-component in section 4.Let's confirm the pieces are healthy:gateway ready login service ready (keycloak) access-control ready (2/2 replicas) sync service ready And let's make sure that everything is configured correctly:gateway: address: http://kaos-gateway.kaos-system.svc.cluster.local through_gateway: true auth: issuer: http://keycloak.keycloak.svc.cluster.local:8080/realms/kaos client_id: kaos realm: kaos broker_url: http://aib-agentic-identity-broker.aib-system.svc.cluster.local:8000 broker_admin_url: http://aib-agentic-identity-broker.aib-system.svc.cluster.local:14000/api namespace: kaos-system sessions: {} The is the actual agent traffic, meaning users invoking agents and agents calling tools and models. Every one of those calls travels through the Gateway Mesh and is checked before it is let through.The hands-on example uses the following resources:two users: (group ) and (group )two agents: (user-activated) and (autonomous agent)one model: (a model endpoint both agents may use)one external service: , covered in section 5The rules are that the group may use the agent, the agent may reach and , and the autonomous may reach . Everything else is denied, including bob (poor bob).Here's a chart that shows what we'll try to accomplish:2.1 How identity flows through a requestEvery call, a user/agent reaching an agent, or a user/agent reaching a tool or model, travels , which does two checks before letting it through:A is like an ID card issued by the identity provider, and both the user and the agent hold one.User Auth issues signed tokens for human users and it carries their groups ( isn't a core OIDC claim, so the identity provider maps it in; with Keycloak that's a group-membership protocol mapper).Agent Auth also issues signed tokens, but an agent starts from a credential it was given (a mounted ServiceAccount token, or a client secret) and exchanges that for one.The gateway does the two checks in order; first it confirms the token is genuine and unexpired (identity), then it asks the KAOS Authz Service whether that identity is allowed to do this (permission), and only if both pass does the request reach its destination.If the authz service the request is denied. There's no config knob to loosen this, since the operator sets on every policy it generates, and it's the reason the authz service runs highly available.2.2 Deploy the agents and toolsEverything the example needs (both agents, the tool, the model, and the access rule for who may use them) is bundled as a single sample. I deploy it with one command, then walk through each object and create it step by step.Here's the one line deploy command:kaos samples deploy 8-authorization-walkthrough -n kaos-system modelapi.kaos.tools/model-api serverside-applied mcpserver.kaos.tools/echo-mcp serverside-applied agent.kaos.tools/researcher serverside-applied agent.kaos.tools/autobot serverside-applied accessgrant.kaos.tools/researchers-to-researcher serverside-applied
Deployed sample '8-authorization-walkthrough' The tool's single function is an echo, and the model's responses are mocked, so every result is deterministic and the walkthrough only exercises . The four resources first, each a plain Kubernetes object (the access rule follows in 2.3):A model endpoint both agents may call.A tool (an MCP server) exposing a single function the may use.A user-facing agent. It needs a person behind it and carries that person's identity through to whatever it calls.An agent. No user behind it; it runs on a schedule and acts as itself.Each resource has its own command, so you can build a similar setup by hand and see the shape of each object. The model and tool first:# a small in-cluster model endpoint kaos modelapi create model-api \ --mode hosted \ --model "smollm2:135m"
# an echo tool exposed as an MCP server kaos mcp create echo-mcp \ --runtime python-string \ --params 'def echo(message: str) -> str: """Echo a note for the authorization walkthrough.""" return f"Echo: {message}"' Then the two agents. Agents acting on behalf of users - on outside servicesWhat happens when the researcher agent needs to access GitHub on behalf of the user? Whose GitHub account does it act on?Everything so far focuses on identity for access control, and nothing yet lets an agent reach external oauth services like GitHub as the specific user instead of through a shared bot account.The naive way to let an agent use GitHub is to give it a single bot account's token and let every user's request ride on it (I did exactly this the first time round). People build it because it's the thing to build, one token in a Secret, one HTTP client, done. But it's a shared credential, so GitHub sees one identity for everyone, you can't tell whose request was whose, and revoking one person's access means rotating the token for all of them. Worse, that durable token now lives somewhere the agent can read.Nothing from sections 1-4 can fix it, because an in-cluster can't express "GitHub as alice". The cluster has no authority over GitHub's tokens, so it can decide a request leaves, but it can't make GitHub see alice instead of the bot. Bridging that gap needs a component that holds each user's GitHub credential (issued by GitHub, consented to by the user) and puts the right one on each outbound call.KAOS does the opposite of the shared bot on all 3 counts. When alice asks the researcher to touch GitHub, GitHub receives token and sees alice, and bob's requests go out as bob, so permissions and audit on the GitHub side are per-person, exactly as if each user called GitHub directly. The agent only ever holds its own short-lived in-cluster identity, because the real GitHub token is swapped onto the outbound request at the gateway and the agent code never touches it. And alice can withdraw her approval at any time without affecting anyone else.5.2 Enter the Agent Identity Broker (AIB)The component that holds each user's real credential is the (AIB; deployed from the chart). Present it proof of who the user is and which agent is acting, and it returns that user's stored third-party token. It never issues anyone's identity; agents get theirs from Agent Auth, users from User Auth, and the AIB only ever trades one proven identity for a stored credential.Nothing new gets installed here. What made this expensive for everyone was that the credential vault and the consent surface were homework each team had to do alone, and that piece has just been open sourced.If your agents can act as your users without ever holding their credentials, identity has become the dull part of the platform, and I think that's exactly where it belongs.Part 1: the problem, what to build on, and the broker. The three questions every agent request has to answer, the standards and tools that already exist, what the Agentic Identity Broker does, and the architecture decisions I made on top of it.Part 2 (this post): agent identity in action. A worked example that runs end to end on a cluster, with two users, two agents, a tool, a model and a third-party service, and real allow and deny outputs.

item.title: Physicists Trap a Single Antimatter Particle For a Month
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Physicists at Northwestern University have successfully trapped a single positron for an entire month, allowing researchers to study its quantum properties with unprecedented precision. "Further investigations using the trap might reveal the secret of why the world around us is made of matter and not antimatter, when things could have presumably gone either way," reports Scientific American. From the report: Every normal particle of matter has an antimatter counterpart with equal mass but opposite charge. To build their trap, physicists started with atoms of sodium 22, a radioactive isotope with a half-life of about two and a half years. When one of these atoms decays, it emits a positron -- the antimatter counterpart of the electron. "The big challenge is to persuade these positrons to slow down and then capture them," says Gerald Gabrielse, a physicist at Northwestern University, who oversaw the project. The team reported its achievement on Wednesday in Physical Review Letters (PDF).
The first step is to send the positrons through the crystal lattice of a sliver of cold tungsten. As the particles go pinballing through the material, they slow down and lose energy. "Every time they bang into something, there's a chance of annihilation, but it doesn't always happen," Gabrielse says. "If they make it to the end, they get popped out." Next, the physicists steer the positrons along a channel using electromagnetic fields. Eventually the particles end up in a vacuum, just three tenths of a degree Celsius above absolute zero, trapped by an electric field on top and bottom and a magnetic field on the sides. "If you want to hold on to antimatter, you have to hold it in a container without walls," Gabrielse says. This method allowed the researchers to isolate and study a solitary, lone positron for a monthâ"and could let them do so indefinitely.
The researchers intend to use their trap to make precise measurements of the positron's magnetic moment -- basically the strength and orientation of its magnetic field. To do this, they must determine two things: the energy needed to flip the direction of the positron's spin and the energy needed to make it jump from its ground state to its first excited state. Using a similar trap setup, Gabrielse and his team have already measured the magnetic moment of an electron to a precision of one part in 10 trillion. Taking the equivalent measurement for a positron will allow them to make a crucial comparison. "We're looking to see if they have an exactly opposite magnetic moment," Gabrielse says. That's the prediction of the Standard Model of particle physics. If the two have different values, however, this could help explain why our universe is made of matter instead of antimatter.

item.title: 1Claw Builds the Security Layer for the Day AI Agents Run Wallets and Sign Trades Autonomously
item.author: Ishan Pandey
item.content:encoded: An AI agent that deploys code, pays an invoice or signs a blockchain transaction usually does it with whatever a human would have used, a private key, an API secret or a cloud credential, sitting in its environment where anything that talks to the model can reach it. One prompt injection or one leaked log hands an attacker everything the agent was allowed to do, at a time when CrowdStrike has watched intruders move from first access to the rest of a network in 27 seconds.1Claw sells a different arrangement in which the agent gets permission to act without receiving the master key, through HSM-backed vaults, per-agent spending limits and an enclave proxy that screens model traffic for prompt injection. It signs transactions across more than 109 EVM chains as well as Bitcoin, Solana, XRP, Cardano and Tron, offers a free tier for developers and has just announced integrations with Bankr, Google Cloud, Circle, Tenderly, Coder and the XRP Ledger.Today we sit down with Kevin Jones, its Founder and CEO and a veteran of Web3 infrastructure, on what security looks like for software that no longer waits for a human to press the button. Hi Kevin, welcome to our "Behind the Startup" series. You went from photography to Web2 infrastructure, then to blockchain and now 1Claw. Tell us about your journey and what problems did you see in the market that made you build 1Claw? Throughout my 25-year career in technology, one thing has always motivated me: figuring out how things work, finding ways to make them better, and solving problems that matter. I've also learned that as technology becomes more powerful, keeping it secure becomes increasingly important.I've worked across companies including Best Buy, Yellow Pages, and NGINX, progressing from Site Reliability Engineer to Solutions Architect. Along the way, I've seen firsthand how complex and fragile technology systems can be, and how a single vulnerability can create serious consequences. Those experiences taught me that security shouldn't be an afterthought. It needs to be part of how we build technology from the beginning.My curiosity about cryptography eventually led me into Web3. I was fascinated by how cryptography, data ownership, and decentralized governance could change the way we establish trust online. I began to see that some of these ideas could also help solve security challenges in traditional Web2 systems. For me, it was never just about blockchain; it was about finding better ways to protect the systems and people who depend on technology.Then AI agents started taking off, and I saw another important challenge emerging. We're moving beyond AI that simply answers questions to AI that can access tools, interact with systems, and take action on our behalf. But these agents often need access to sensitive credentials and APIs to do their jobs. If that access isn't properly controlled, the consequences can be serious. I saw an opportunity to apply what I'd learned over the years to help address a problem that will only become more important as AI evolves.That's what inspired me to create 1Claw. I want to help make AI agents safer to use by giving organizations better control over what they can access and do, while still allowing them to be useful and autonomous. I believe we shouldn't have to choose between innovation and security. We should be able to embrace what AI makes possible while building the safeguards that let people trust it.Ultimately, what drives me is the opportunity to solve meaningful problems and help make technology work better for everyone. AI has enormous potential, and I want to help ensure that potential can be realized safely.Outside of technology, photography has always been my creative outlet. It reminds me to slow down, look at things differently, and appreciate the beauty in the world around us. I think that same curiosity carries over into my work: whether I'm behind a camera or solving a complex technical problem, I'm always looking for a new perspective.How 1Claw Signs a Transaction Without Handing Over the Key You mention that the agent gets permission to act but not the master key. Could you walk us through what actually happens, step by step, when an agent asks 1Claw to sign a transaction or call a paid API on its behalf? The idea is simple: an AI agent should be able to get work done without ever having unrestricted access to the credentials that make it possible.Let's say an agent needs to call a paid API or sign a transaction. Instead of handing the agent a permanent API key or private key, 1Claw acts as a controlled security layer between the agent and the resource it needs.Here's how it works, step by step.First, the agent requests an action. It might need to call an API, access a service, or initiate a blockchain transaction.Second, 1Claw verifies the agent's identity and checks its permissions. Is this agent authorized to perform this action? Does it have access to this particular service? Are there restrictions on what it can do?Third, 1Claw applies the relevant security policies. Depending on the configuration, that could mean limiting which credentials the agent can use, which actions it can perform, or what resources it can access.Fourth, if the request is authorized, 1Claw facilitates access to the required credential or signing capability without giving the agent unrestricted control of the underlying secret. For a paid API, that could mean enabling an authorized API call without exposing the long-lived credential. For a blockchain transaction, it could mean routing a signing request through a protected signing mechanism, subject to the applicable permissions.Finally, the action proceeds within those boundaries, and the organization can maintain visibility into how access is being used.The important distinction is that the agent gets permission to perform a specific action, not a master key that gives it unlimited power.That's the philosophy behind 1Claw: give agents the access they need to be useful, while keeping control of sensitive credentials and permissions outside the agent itself.What Fails First When Attackers Move at Machine Speed CrowdStrike says AI-enabled adversaries increased their operations by 89% last year and the fastest breakout it recorded took 27 seconds. When attackers move at machine speed, which part of a company's security stack fails first? And how do companies build new cybersecurity rails?The first thing that breaks is often the assumption that humans can keep up. Traditional security relies heavily on people detecting unusual activity, investigating alerts, and responding to threats. But when attackers operate at machine speed, manual processes and fragmented security systems can struggle to keep pace.AI agents introduce another challenge: they don't just process information; they can take action across multiple systems using credentials and permissions. If those credentials are compromised or an agent is manipulated, the potential impact can spread quickly.Companies need a new security layer built for autonomous systems. That means giving every agent a verifiable identity, enforcing least-privilege access, protecting credentials, monitoring actions, and being able to revoke access quickly when something goes wrong.At 1Claw, we're focused on this access-control problem: helping organizations manage what AI agents can access and do without exposing sensitive credentials or giving them unnecessary permissions.When threats move at machine speed, security can't depend on humans reacting fast enough. It has to be built into the infrastructure from the start.What Agents Can Safely Do Through Bankr, Circle, Tenderly and Coder Bankr and Circle put agents next to real money, Tenderly simulates transactions before they are signed and Coder hands coding agents a cloud workspace. What can an agent do safely through these integrations today that it could not do a year ago? The big shift is that AI agents are moving from making recommendations to taking real actions. With platforms like Bankr and Circle, agents can interact with wallets and move money. Tenderly lets developers simulate transactions before signing them, while Coder gives coding agents controlled environments to write and execute code.That means agents can now participate in real financial and development workflows with safeguards that weren't as accessible a year ago.But enabling an agent to act is only half the problem. How do you make sure it can do only what it's supposed to do? Simulating a transaction or isolating a workspace helps, but neither automatically prevents an agent from accessing the wrong credentials or exercising excessive permissions.That's where 1Claw comes in. We're focused on helping organizations control which credentials, APIs, and tools their agents can access, limit their permissions, and revoke access when needed.The future isn't about giving agents unlimited autonomy. It's about giving them the authority to get work done without giving them the keys to everything.Protecting the Moment of Approval When an Agent Decides Alone The FBI attributed the $1.5 billion Bybit theft to North Korea after attackers fooled the people approving a transaction rather than breaking the keys. If the weakest point is the moment of approval, how do you protect a decision that an agent makes on its own?The $1.5 billion Bybit theft exposed a critical weakness in security: attackers can exploit the process used to approve a transaction, even when the underlying systems have strong protections. The FBI attributed the attack to North Korea, highlighting how manipulating a trusted workflow can have devastating consequences.With AI agents, the challenge is even greater: how do you secure a decision when the agent makes it autonomously? You can't rely on the agent to recognize every malicious instruction or judge whether its own actions are safe.The answer is to separate the agent's ability to request an action from the authority to execute it. Every request should be checked against independent security policies: What is the agent trying to do? Does it have permission? Is the action within its limits? If not, it should be blocked. High-risk actions can also require human approval.That's what we're focused on at 1Claw: giving agents the access they need to get work done without giving them unrestricted authority over credentials, APIs, and critical systems.The principle is simple: let agents make decisions, but make sure security controls, not the agents themselves, determine what they're allowed to do.Revoking a Misbehaving Agent at 3 AM and Who Is Accountable Imagine an agent starts misbehaving at three in the morning while nobody on the team is watching. How fast can a company revoke it through 1Claw and who is accountable for what it has already done? If an AI agent starts misbehaving at three in the morning, the company shouldn't have to wait for someone to wake up to contain it. Access needs to be revocable as soon as a problem is detected, cutting off the agent's ability to use protected credentials and resources. The exact response time depends on how the system is configured and where the agent is operating.With 1Claw, our focus is giving organizations control over what agents can access and do, including the ability to revoke their permissions when necessary. Just as importantly, revocation doesn't erase what an agent has already done. That's why visibility and auditability matter: organizations need to understand which actions were taken, what resources were accessed, and which permissions allowed them.Revoking access is a technical control; accountability is an organizational responsibility. The company deploying the agent remains responsible for its permissions, policies, and oversight. 1Claw's role is to help make access controllable and actions traceable, so organizations can contain incidents and understand what happened.Autonomous agents may operate around the clock, but security and accountability can't depend on someone being awake to supervise every action.The Key Lesson Crypto Learned That AI Is About to Repeat Last question. Which lesson about keys did crypto learn the hard way that the rest of the AI industry is about to learn all over again? The biggest lesson crypto learned the hard way is that whoever controls the keys controls everything, and if those keys are compromised, the damage can be irreversible. In Web3, we saw billions of dollars lost through stolen private keys, exposed credentials, compromised wallets, and poorly managed access. The technology could be incredibly sophisticated, but security often came down to a simple question: who holds the keys, and what can they do with them?Now we're seeing a similar challenge emerge with AI agents. We're giving agents access to APIs, credentials, databases, and business systems so they can act autonomously. But if an agent has unrestricted access, gets manipulated, or exposes its credentials, the consequences can extend far beyond a single task.The lesson crypto learned is that securing the technology isn't enough. You have to secure access to the technology.That's one of the ideas behind 1Claw. AI agents need credentials to be useful, but they shouldn't have unlimited access to everything those credentials unlock. We need to control what agents can access, limit their permissions, protect their secrets, and be able to revoke access when something goes wrong.Crypto learned that key management isn't a secondary security feature; it's fundamental infrastructure. The AI industry has an opportunity to learn that lesson before compromised agents turn it into another expensive one.Don’t forget to like and share the story!

item.title: We Were Never Asked to Write Code. We Were Asked to Solve Problems.
item.author: Sanya Kapoor
item.content:encoded: In 2000 I was at Deutsche Bank, building a new trading platform, watching friends leave one by one for startups that were going to make them rich. They had stock options. They had retirement mapped out at forty. I stayed at the bank and felt the envy of a man doing sensible work while everyone around him seemed to be getting away with something.Then the crash came, and the turned out to be nothing. Pets.com went from a Super Bowl advert in January to liquidation in November. The Nasdaq lost most of its value. Thousands of companies died; the web did not. It carried on and built Google. I was still at the bank, and I have rarely been so grateful for a boring decision.I mention this because I have seen the current mood before, and I recognise the smell.The oldest trick in the industry“Artificial intelligence” is a marketing term. It was coined in the 1950s by scientists who wanted money from the American military, and it worked—which is the only reason we still say it. Every decade or so the phrase gets dusted off, oversold, and followed by an “AI winter” when the funding leaves. We are on the fourth or fifth turn of that wheel, depending on how you count.The technology underneath is real. Deep learning did something startling at the ImageNet competition in 2012, and within three years your phone could identify what was in a photograph. But real capability and honest expectation are different things, and the gap between them is where the money is made.The pattern never changes. A genuine breakthrough arrives, and capital floods in behind it. The promises inflate to justify the valuations until someone is on a stage telling you half your engineers will be redundant by Tuesday. Then reality turns up, the money leaves, and the people still standing go back to work.The radiologists who never disappearedIn 2016, Geoffrey Hinton—one of the people who built this technology—told a room that we should stop training radiologists because deep learning would beat them inside five years. He was mistaken. Cheaper, faster imaging meant doctors ordered far more of it, and demand for radiologists climbed. When a task gets cheap and quick, we tend to want more of it, not less.I think about that every time someone tells me my profession is finished. The tools have landed for software this time. In 2025 the agentic coding assistants stopped being a party trick and started closing real work—taking an issue, writing the code, and opening a pull request you can then argue with. My engineers use them. They ship faster for it.What has not happened is anyone being replaced. The tool still needs an adult in the room. Someone who can tell a plausible answer from the right one and who is on call when it falls over at 9:31 on a Monday. That adult is an engineer. There is simply more demand now for the problems we can afford to solve.The point we keep forgettingDeepMind did not write conventional software to crack protein folding, a problem that had defeated biologists for fifty years. It built a model that solved it, then published the structures of 200 million proteins for free. New antibiotics and malaria vaccine research have already come out of that one act. Nobody asked how many lines of code it took.That is the lesson under the noise. We were never hired to write code—the code was always the means. The job was to solve someone’s problem, and it still is.I have spent twenty-odd years mistaking the one for the other, and the machines have done me the favour of pointing it out.Richard Forss is CTO of , a global multi-asset prime broker, where he leads a 230-person technology division—none of whom he has yet worked out how to replace with a machine, himself included.

item.title: StealC Is Back, and This Time It's a RAT
item.author: Varonis
item.content:encoded:
Four months after Operation Endgame took it down, StealC's seller returns with Stadia, a remote access trojan that shares StealC's code byte for byte.In June, Europol tore down StealC, a prominent infostealer, as part of Operation Endgame. International authorities seized 326 servers and 142 domains, recovered more than 25 million stolen credentials from 385,000 infected machines, and pulled the plug on one of the most widely sold infostealers of the last three years.Four months later, on October 16, the seller behind StealC resurfaced with Stadia. This time it's not a stealer: it's a full remote access trojan. The RAT’s features include hidden desktop control, a live command shell, a file explorer, a process manager and an in-memory loader, with StealC's stealer welded on as one module among six. The actor behind Stadia is working hard to win back original StealC customers: every former StealC customer is offered a free month on the top ($900) tier.Varonis Threat Labs obtained the build shortly after it was listed, reversed it, and watched its panel operate against a machine of our own. The code inside it is StealC's.Operation Endgame forced the seller to rebuild its infrastructure and start again with a new name, new servers and a new panel. This blog walks through that rebuild from the inside: the listing, the panel running against a host of our own, the agent's code, and the detections that catch it.The listing is titled [RAT] Stadia - Stealer, Log Restore, Loader, HVNC, File Explorer (HVNC is Hidden Virtual Network Computing, remote desktop control the victim cannot see), and the seller pitches it as an agent that embeds itself in the system and hands the operator a full toolkit from a web panel.The module list reads like a remote administration suite rather than a stealer:with two modes, a shared desktop and a hidden desktop, described as self-written and not based on public sourcesa custom solution on the base of their stealc v3.5cmd.exe access with input/output streaminga resident loader that runs files from disk or from memoryremote disk access to browse, download, upload and run filesa process tree with the ability to kill a competitor's processThe stealer collects from 50+ browsers, 120+ crypto plugins, 50+ desktop wallets, messengers (Telegram, Discord, Tox, Pidgin), Steam, Battle.net, Uplay and Roblox sessions, Outlook and Thunderbird, and ProtonVPN and OpenVPN clients. A wallet brute covers MetaMask, TronLink, Trust, Phantom, Rabby, OKX and others.The seller's own screenshots in the listing show the product in use. Their demo dashboard reports 596 hosts and 496 logs, with a world map of infections concentrated in South and Southeast Asia, Africa and Latin America.The logs view carries the StealC heritage on its face: per-victim rows with wallet and extension tags, country, OS and a download button for the archive.The HVNC screenshot is a live remote-desktop session on an infected Windows 11 machine, with a Spanish-language runtime error dialog sitting on the victim's desktop. The seller's toolbar offers Ctrl+Alt+Del, Win+R, quality settings and a full-screen mode.Pricing and the StealC pipelineStadia sells on a monthly subscription, tiered by how many modules and builds you get.up to 5 builds, up to 5 accountsHVNC, Remote CMD, Stealer, Loader, File Explorer, Process Managerno build or account limitA second post, added a minute after the listing, offers every StealC customer a free month on the Pro tier. Customers whose panels and servers went down in June get the fuller toolkit at no cost, and the seller keeps the install base.Buyers run everything from a web panel. It brands itself Stadia and runs at version 1.1.2, matching the agent version baked into the sample. Its news tab is a short changelog. Update 1.0.0 (10 Sep 2026) is the first beta release. Update 1.1.0 (29 Sep 2026) records the Stealer module code updated to stealc 3.5.0.The builder tab compiles agents from the current published version. Operators create a build, download the .exe, and deploy it. Our sample is one such build.The sidebar organizes stolen data by type: passwords, credit cards, messengers, software, session tokens for Chrome, Discord, Steam, Roblox, and Azure, and a crypto section for seed phrases.To see the agent and panel as a pair, we stood up one disposable Windows host of our own and let it register. It appeared in the panel's host inventory within a minute, tagged online.The host overview is a full remote-administration console: live status and heartbeat, the install path under C:\ProgramData\, counters for passwords, cookies, wallets, cards and files, related tasks and logs, and a Start Module menu offering Remote CMD, File Explorer, Process Manager, Remote Desktop, Loader and Stealer.Starting a module opens a confirmation dialog first. Remote Desktop offers a current-desktop or isolated virtual-desktop session.The Loader accepts EXE, PowerShell, CMD and MSI, with disk or in-memory execution for each. A job targets selected hosts or every matching host.The log it produced for our host carried a system profile, a desktop screenshot and build metadata, with zero credentials because the host was clean. The archive layout (build.txt, copyright.txt, screenshot.jpg, system_info.txt) is the StealC log format.The sample we pulled from that builder is a 560,128-byte 32-bit Windows executable, native Microsoft Visual C++ (MSVC), no .NET, no Authenticode signature. It decrypts its own build marker to STADIA_BETA and reports agent version 1.1.2, so the file and the panel agree on what it is.ea928494fd30d88b98141d39a502a4324889fb732e74b44bfee12c72137dd73e028afae8b5e9953e1cd84a003c42fd85There is no packer. The outer file imports only KERNEL32.dll and resolves nearly every operational application programming interface (API) at runtime, so the static picture stays thin until you decrypt the strings.Almost every meaningful literal (module names, command-and-control (C2) fields, the config) is stored under one scheme: stored literal = Base64(RC4(plaintext, "eepkTOgSwdNCgrhITR")) The outer Rivest Cipher 4 (RC4) key sits at file offset 0x6B1A0. Recovering the table is a few lines of Python once you have the key: Base64-decode each candidate, RC4 it with the key, keep anything that comes out printable. def rc4(data, key): s = list(range(256)) j = 0 for i in range(256): j = (j + s[i] + key[i % len(key)]) & 0xFF s[i], s[j] = s[j], s[i] i = j = 0 out = bytearray() for b in data: i = (i + 1) & 0xFF j = (j + s[i]) & 0xFF s[i], s[j] = s[j], s[i] out.append(b ^ s[(s[i] + s[j]) & 0xFF]) return bytes(out)
# stored = Base64(RC4(plaintext, key)); recover with: # plaintext = rc4(base64.b64decode(stored), b"eepkTOgSwdNCgrhITR") That pass returns 542 strings: the command vocabulary, the browser targets, the scheduled-task template and the C2 config. The message key and access token were recovered but are omitted from this write-up.Startup and the locale gateEntry is ordinary MSVC startup into a WinMain-like routine. Early on, the agent calls GetUserDefaultLangID and exits for Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian, Kazakh, and Uzbek system languages (0x0419, 0x0422, 0x0423, 0x043F, 0x0443), the standard do-not-run-at-home guard. It then checks whether its own path sits under C:\ProgramData\. If not, it installs; if so, it takes a single-instance mutex Local\<username>.<computername> and enters the agent loop.That branch is why our one dynamic run went nowhere. Launched under a Low-integrity token from outside ProgramData, the sample took the installer path, could not create its directory, and exited silently. That result reflects our lab setup and says nothing about whether the sample works.How it talks to the serverOnce installed, the agent calls home. The config carries three hard-coded C2 bases, all plain HTTP on the root path:http://93.152.213.215/http://91.92.43.45/The agent tries its three C2 addresses in a fixed order, starting with the first every time it reconnects. To test each one, it sends a set_online message with a host_token of 72 zeroes and waits up to eight seconds for any reply that contains an opcode. If none of the three answers, it waits 300 seconds and starts again.The traffic is not what its header claims. Each message starts as JSON, is encrypted with RC4 using the embedded message key, and is then Base64-encoded before being sent as the HTTP body. The request still declares Content-Type: application/json, so anything inspecting the header expects JSON and receives ciphertext.Persistence, modules and injectionInstallation drops the agent under a randomized 12-character directory below C:\ProgramData\ and picks a filename from a fixed list of nine that impersonate legitimate updaters:OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exeThe scheduled task name is selected separately from the same nine names, so the task label and the executable need not match. The task is hidden, runs at logon and every 15 minutes for 3,650 days. When the agent is elevated, it also issues a hidden PowerShell Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath for its install directory. Our test host confirms the scheme: it installed to C:\ProgramData\wzoHcrvZt9RX\MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe, a 12-character directory and one of the nine names.The decrypted module vocabulary matches the panel one-to-one:hidden shell, bidirectional stdin/stdoutlist, read, write, pull, push, run; chunked transferprocess tree, CPU/RAM, kill, protected-process listcurrent or virtual desktop, JPEG frames, full input injectionEXE, PowerShell, BAT/CMD, MSI; disk or memory; hidden or runasbrowser profiles, cookies, logins, walletsThe seller says the stealer is built on StealC 3.5. The binary proves the two share code at the byte level.Inside stadia_x32.exe, at file offset 0x77D48, sits a complete 26,112-byte (0x6600) 64-bit Chromium App-Bound Encryption helper, a mapped portable executable (PE) plus a short reflective loader. That exact blob appears once in each of the StealC v3.5 x86 and x64 builds we hold, byte for byte:0e5337a4cc8ebc772bc50f6e79befd1e8efad3410022e050d08d5269733c4ea4StealC v3.5 build_x32.exe0e5337a4cc8ebc772bc50f6e79befd1e8efad3410022e050d08d5269733c4ea4StealC v3.5 build_x64.exe0e5337a4cc8ebc772bc50f6e79befd1e8efad3410022e050d08d5269733c4ea4Stadia's C2 addresses, RC4 key and access token change with every build. What stays the same is how the agent talks to its server and what it does on the host, and that is where detection should focus.On the network, the agent sends HTTP POST requests to the root path of a bare IP address. The Content-Type header claims the body is JSON, but the body is Base64-encoded ciphertext. That mismatch is a useful signal on its own. The build we analyzed calls 93.152.213.215, 91.92.43.45 and 193.148.56.97 on port 80, and blocking those addresses covers that build only.On the host, the clearest signal is the browser credential theft. An unsigned process running from C:\ProgramData\ starts a genuine Chrome, Edge or Brave process in a suspended state and writes a 26 KB block of code into it. Moments later, a .txt file with a GUID-style name appears in C:\ProgramData\, holds a 64-character hex string, and is deleted. That file carries the key the browser uses to protect saved cookies and passwords.Persistence leaves its own trail. Within a few minutes of infection, look for a new executable in a random folder under C:\ProgramData\, a hidden scheduled task that repeats every 15 minutes, and a Windows Defender exclusion added for that folder through PowerShell's Add-MpPreference command. This Sigma rule flags the scheduled task: title: Hidden Fifteen Minute Scheduled Task Executes From ProgramData status: experimental logsource: product: windows service: security detection: selection_event: EventID: [4698, 4702] selection_xml: TaskContent|contains|all: - '<Interval>PT15M</Interval>' - '<Duration>P3650D</Duration>' - '<Hidden>true</Hidden>' - 'C:\ProgramData\' condition: selection_event and selection_xml level: high The implant registers the task through the Component Object Model (COM) API, so a rule scoped to schtasks.exe would miss it. Start the behavioral rules in alert mode and tune them against your own telemetry before you block on them.Stadia is the StealC operation rebuilding after Operation Endgame. The servers, domains and stolen data are gone, and the response has been to come back under a new name with a broader product and a free month to pull former customers across. The stealer is still there, now as one module in a remote access trojan that adds hidden VNC, a command shell, a file explorer, a process manager and in-memory loading.StealC took credentials and left. item.title: MEXC Account Types Explained: A Guide to Spot, Futures, RealStocks, Fiat, and Copy Trade Accounts
item.author: MEXC Learn
item.content:encoded: ● MEXC organizes accounts by function, including Spot, Futures, Fiat, Copy Trade, Earn, RealStocks, Prediction Markets, and Trading Bot accounts.● Spot, Futures, Fiat, and Copy Trade are the four core account types beginners are most likely to use.● Funds can be transferred between different accounts depending on how you use them, with the Fiat account used for fiat-to-crypto and crypto-to-fiat conversions.● Transfers between MEXC accounts are free, allowing you to move funds whenever needed.● Both the MEXC website and App support quick fund transfers and let you view your transfer history at any time.1. What Account Types Does MEXC Offer?MEXC organizes its accounts by function. The main typesinclude Spot, Futures, Fiat, and Copy Trade accounts, as well as Earn, RealStocks, Prediction Markets, and Trading Bot accounts. Of these, Spot, Futures, Fiat, and Copy Trade are the four core account types beginners are most likely to use.2. What Is Each Account Used For?** This account is used for Spot trading. When you buy or sell crypto on MEXC’s Spot market, the assets used for trading are held in your Spot account. This account is used for Futures trading, including contracts with different margin types. Funds used for Futures trading are held in this account. This account is used to move funds into and out of MEXC. Conversions from fiat currency to crypto, or from crypto back to fiat currency, are handled through this account. This account holds funds used for copy trading. When you follow a lead trader, the system automatically places orders for you based on that trader’s strategy, and the trader can receive a share of your profits. Although copy trading is a form of Futures trading, its assets are held separately in the Copy Trade account.MEXC also offers for assets allocated to Earn products, for RealStocks trading, Prediction Markets accounts for prediction market trading, and for automated strategy trading, supporting a range of asset management needs.3. How Are the Different Accounts Connected?To understand how the accounts are connected, follow how funds move between them:When you start trading, you first convert fiat currency into crypto. The converted assets are held in your Fiat account.For Spot trading, transfer funds from your Fiat account to your Spot account. For Futures trading, transfer them to your Futures account. The same principle applies to Earn, RealStocks, Prediction Markets, and Trading Bot activities, withfunds transferred directly between your Spot account and the relevant account as needed.To trade RealStocks or participate in market predictions, transfer funds to your RealStocks or Prediction Markets account. Both support direct transfers to and from your Spot account.For copy trading, first transfer assets from your Futures or Fiat account to your Spot account. Once you confirm your copy trading settings, the system automatically transfers the specified amount from your Spot account to your Copy Trade account.When you subscribe to an Earn product, the system transfers the specified amount to your Earn account. After redemption, the funds are returned to the corresponding account.To use a trading bot for automated strategy trading, create and start a strategy, such as grid trading. The system then transfers the specified amount to your Trading Bot account.When you stop trading and are ready to cash out, transfer the crypto in your accounts back to your Fiat account, then convert it into fiat currency to complete the withdrawal.4. Are There Fees for Transfers Between Accounts?No. Transfers between MEXC accounts are free. You can move funds as needed for trading without paying any additional transfer fees.5. How to Transfer Funds Between AccountsApp: From the MEXC App home screen, tap Wallets → Overview / Spot / RealStocks / Futures / Fiat / Prediction Markets → Transferto move funds between accounts.Transfers to a Copy Trade account must be made through the copy trading page. Funds remain in your Spot account until you submit your copy trading settings. The system then transfers the specified amount to your Copy Trade account.The same applies to Earn and Trading Bot accounts. The system only transfers the specified amount to the relevant account once you subscribe to an Earn product or participate in grid trading.6. How to View and Manage Each Account’s Funding HistoryWeb: Go to the , then select the tab to view your transfer history.App: From the MEXC App home screen, tap Wallets → Overview → Transfer → to view your transfer history.To view details for an individual account, select it on the page. The account page shows information such as total assets, crypto holdings, and profit and loss analysis, and provides options to deposit, withdraw, and transfer funds.Understanding MEXC’s account types and how to transfer assets between them can help you move funds quickly and trade more efficiently.

item.title: Your Agent Workflow Is Mostly Code and People
item.author: Sakti Bagchi
item.content:encoded: On 3rd October, my astro-coach agent tried to fix a production Supabase environment problem. It kept retrying until a model usage limit stopped it. The tempting summary is “the agent tried to fix production.”That summary hides most of the engineering.Step in the 3 October astro-coach runDiagnose the production Supabase environment problemA diagnosis and a specific fix to attemptBake the environment settings into the application buildA build artifact whose configuration needed verificationAn unresolved execution state the agent could not readDecide to retry the environment fixModel, acting through the agentAnother invocation, without resolving the previous attempt’s stateKeep retrying until a model usage limit stopped the runModel choosing retries; code executing themAn interrupted workflow, without a confirmed outcomeConfirm the login message and whether users could actually log inThe evidence needed to accept the fix or keep the incident openThis was a workflow on my astro-coach repository, now home to Jyotish Coach. It is tempting to summarize it as “the agent tried to fix production.”That description hides most of the engineering.A person supplied the diagnosis. Code performed the environment bake. The model chose to repeat the operation. A person still needed to confirm the result.The agent’s consequential contribution was the decision at the boundary: run that step again.Most of what we call an agent workflow is a chain of ordinary software operations and human decisions, with a model choosing some of the transitions. If you ship agents, those transitions deserve as much attention as the model.Where the loop actually livedThe environment bake was a code operation. Given the intended configuration and a source revision, the build system should produce an artifact and report what happened.The repository makes this distinction concrete. Its Dockerfile passes and NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY into the environment before running the application build.Its operations notes also warn that, in this deployment setup, changing those variables and triggering a redeploy can reuse the previous image. The documented check is to look for an actual application build.That means “the variable changed,” “the deployment completed,” and “the browser received the intended configuration” are separate claims.After the hang in the 3rd October run, the agent could not read the execution state. It kept attempting the production environment fix until a model usage limit stopped it.The loop lived around the code operation: invoke, lose visibility, invoke again.A hang does not tell you whether an operation failed before making a change, completed without returning a response, or remained in progress. Repeating the command does not resolve that uncertainty. It can add another attempt whose relationship to the first is also unclear.The usage limit ended the activity. It did not establish that production was correct.“Agent fixed it” is too coarse to review. Each handoff needs an input, a record of the state left behind, and a next owner.For this workflow, I would name them explicitly:Input crossing the boundaryThe person’s diagnosis, target environment, and intended configuration changeA proposed operation with a defined scopeModel prepares the action; person reviews its scopeApproved inputs and source revisionAn identified build attempt and its logsBuild → deployment approvalArtifact identity and configuration checksA report of success, failure, or unresolved executionApproval → production changeSign-off tied to that artifact and targetA deployment attempt with a recorded identityInterrupted execution → reconciliationAttempt identity and last known statusA read-only determination of what happened, or an explicit unknownCode checks state; person owns unresolved casesDeployment → login acceptanceThe deployed revision and technical checksEvidence from the actual sign-in flowThis is a proposed ownership structure, not a claim that the October run followed it. The run exposed why it was needed.The weakest handoff was interrupted execution to the next decision. The agent had an incomplete observation, but retained the ability to initiate another production attempt.That is where uncertainty became action.A durable attempt record would make a different next step possible: inspect the existing operation. Without that record, the model is being asked to reason about state it cannot observe.Make the environment bake a script that runs once and reportsThe structural fix is to take the repeated environment bake out of the model’s decision loop.I would make it a script that runs once for a specified operation, then reports. Its inputs would identify the source revision, target environment, and intended configuration. Its output would identify the build attempt, resulting artifact, verification results, and final status. It should report configuration checks without exposing secret values.“Runs once” needs enforcement in code. An operation identifier should prevent a second invocation from silently starting duplicate work. If the caller loses its connection, the next action should retrieve that operation’s status.The script also needs to preserve uncertainty honestly. A timeout is an unresolved result until the underlying build or deployment state has been checked.The model can help prepare inputs and interpret the report. The execution contract belongs in code.Before a production change, a person signs off on the concrete artifact, target, and expected effect. That approval must refer to what will actually be deployed. If the artifact changes, the earlier approval no longer describes the action.This gives the workflow a stopping condition tied to the task: a reported result, a verified state, or an unresolved case handed to a person. A model usage limit should never have to serve as the incident’s stopping rule.The step I would not delegateThe final handoff is deployment evidence to user acceptance.A build can succeed with the wrong configuration. A deployment can be healthy while authentication fails. A sign-in message can appear successful without giving the user a usable session.The repository’s authentication environment code documents one such failure mode: sign-in can appear to work while subsequent API calls return unauthorized responses. That is why a reassuring message is insufficient evidence.Automated checks should cover login. They should verify session creation and access to protected routes. But for closing this production incident, I would keep a person responsible for the acceptance decision.I would open the deployed site, use the relevant sign-in method, read the message, and confirm that the session lets me reach the protected experience.The model can assemble evidence. Code can test the path. I would not delegate the final confirmation that users can actually log in.

item.title: UN Says Breaching 1.5C Warming Limit Is 'Imminent and Unavoidable'
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
For the first time, the UN has declared that exceeding the Paris Agreement's 1.5C warming limit is "imminent and unavoidable." "We are now saying this window has closed, but we can open it again by making the overshoot as brief as possible," UN Environment Program Executive Director Inger Andersen said on a call with reporters. "This is about how to find a way back as shortly and as quickly as possible with as limited an overshoot as possible." CNN reports: Past reports have examined the distance between countries' emissions reduction commitments and what it would take to limit global warming to 1.5 C above preindustrial levels. However, this year's report redefines the gap. Instead, it examines new emissions overshoot scenarios, and what it would take to limit peak warming to just 1.7 to 1.8 degrees C before bringing temperatures back down to 1.5 C through emissions cuts and the use of carbon removal technologies.
The report makes clear that every additional fraction of a degree of warming above 1.5 C "raises the risk of irreversible changes including in ice sheets, permafrost carbon, ocean circulation, and coral systems, along with devastating human impacts." Each added fraction of a degree of warming can have an "immense" impact "as measured in terms of damage, cost and loss of lives," said climate scientist Michael Mann of the University of Pennsylvania. Mann was not involved in producing the UNEP report.
According to the UNEP, which is based in Nairobi, the lowest overshoot scenario would keep peak warming to between 1.7 and 1.8 degrees C and return global average temperatures to at or below 1.5 C by 2100. However, to follow such a pathway, global greenhouse gas emissions would need to be slashed by far more than anything currently on the table at the upcoming COP31 talks. This would require an 18% cut by 2030, 45% by 2035, and 69% by 2040, relative to 2025 levels.
Meeting this lowest-possible overshoot scenario would require a tripling of renewable electricity capacity by 2035, and dramatic cuts to fossil fuels, including the phaseout of coal by 2040, the report states. In addition, there would need to be a major scaling up of carbon removal technologies, which so far have not been proven to work at such a large scale. In stark contrast to these figures, the fulfillment of existing emissions reduction pledges would only yield a 5-to-8% emissions cut by 2030 and an 11-to-15% reduction by 2035, the report found. This would be associated with a peak warming of about 2.6 degrees C.
If countries simply follow their current policies, then warming could reach a peak of about 2.8 C. That estimate has increased since last year, in part because of the withdrawal of the United States from the Paris Agreement and retraction of its emissions reduction commitments, the report states. Even the scenario that assumes countries meet their existing reduction commitments, and nations with net-zero pledges succeed in fulfilling them, still brings warming to a peak of 2.1 C.

But money isn't necessarily enough to solve this problem, one source said, because of how quickly the technology is developing and revealing new weaknesses in real time. item.title: To Make Way For Data Centers, Google Will Pay Others to Use Less Power
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Google is funding one of the nation's largest "virtual power plants," paying homes and businesses indirectly to reduce electricity consumption during periods of peak demand so more grid capacity can be available for data centers. Under its expanded deal with Voltus, the program could provide up to 1,070 megawatts in the Mid-Atlantic PJM grid -- roughly the output of a large nuclear reactor. The New York Times reports: That electricity won't come from new power plants. Instead, Voltus will sign up homes and businesses and give them financial incentives to curb their usage when local power demand is high or the grid is strained. Many of these reductions could occur automatically, such as through smart thermostats that dial back air-conditioning during peak summer hours or batteries that can provide temporary on-site power.
Each of these tweaks frees up only a small amount of power on its own. But by aggregating them across thousands of businesses and homes, Voltus says it can reliably provide lots of extra capacity when it's most needed, and do so within a few years. While tech companies will likely ultimately need to build traditional power plants if they want to keep building large data centers, this approach could be a faster, cheaper and less-polluting option in the interim. "We really see virtual power plants as a critical short-term solution," said Ellen Zuckerman, head of energy market development for North and South America at Google. "It's a way to invest in our communities, really double down on our clean energy ambition, but also meet capacity at speed and scale."

item.title: Microsoft Says October Updates Didn't Actually Fix VPN Issues
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
joshuark shares a report from BleepingComputer: Microsoft says it mistakenly flagged a bug causing Always On VPN connection issues as fixed in the October 2026 Windows 11 cumulative updates. Always On VPN replaced the legacy DirectAccess technology and supports domain-joined, non-domain-joined, and Microsoft Entra ID-joined devices running Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server. It runs in the background and establishes secure tunnels back to the user's corporate network whenever their device connects to the internet.
Microsoft first acknowledged the issue in a service alert sent to IT administrators in late September, saying it was triggered on systems running Windows 11 24H2 and later after installing the September 2026 security updates when the initial Always On VPN connection failed (e.g., when using automatic protocol selection with IKEv2 and SSTP). "When automatic protocol selection or protocol fallback was configured, affected VPN connections could remain stuck in a Connecting state or fail to connect after an initial connection attempt failed," it said. "In some cases, subsequent connection attempts could display the error, 'The specified port is already in use.'"
After releasing the October 2026 Patch Tuesday Windows 11 cumulative updates, Microsoft marked the bug as resolved, but in a Tuesday update it said the issues weren't actually addressed and that a fix would ship later. "This disclosure was mistakenly updated to Resolved status on October 13, 2026. We have returned its status to Mitigated," it said in a service alert sent to IT admins. "A resolution for this issue is planned to be included in an update to be released in the coming weeks. We apologize for any inconvenience or confusion." While Microsoft continues working on a permanent solution, it shared a temporary fix that requires affected customers to choose one of two VPN tunneling protocols to work around the issue.
